title: Krylov complexity of anyons
authors: Ya-Nan Wang, Qing-Min Hu, Wen-Long You, Gaoyong Sun
abstract: Anyons obey fractional statistics that lie between bosonic and fermionic statistics, giving rise to a broad range of intriguing phenomena. However, how anyonic statistics govern quantum-state complexity is still largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate the interplay between the statistical phase and on-site interactions in the anyon-Hubbard model, identifying exact quantum many-body scar eigenstates and novel quench dynamics. The Krylov complexity exhibits perfect periodic revivals independent of the statistical phase in the scarred dynamics, whereas after a quench it depends on both the statistical phase and the interaction strength. In the strong-interaction regime, we find approximate scarred dynamics, while in the weak-interaction regime the state spreads over Krylov space and the complexity ultimately saturates. Moreover, for the bosonic initial state, the complexity of fermions exhibits the lowest saturation value, and vice versa. For fractional statistics, the saturation plateau is minimized when the post-quench statistical phase is close to that of the initial state. Our results demonstrate the central role of the statistical phase in governing many-body dynamics and provide new insights into Krylov complexity and quantum many-body scars.
summary: The paper analyzes the anyon-Hubbard model to understand how fractional statistics influence quantum state complexity. Using Krylov complexity, the authors show that while scarred dynamics exhibit phase-independent revivals, quench dynamics are highly sensitive to the statistical phase and interaction strength. This highlights the central role of exotic statistics in governing many-body non-equilibrium behavior.
main_problem: The work investigates how anyonic statistics govern quantum-state complexity by studying the interplay between statistical phase and on-site interactions in the anyon-Hubbard model.
main_result: Krylov complexity shows perfect periodic revivals during scarred dynamics, but its behavior after a quench depends critically on both the initial and final statistical phases and interaction strength.
method: The study employs Krylov complexity analysis ($C_K(t)$) and entanglement entropy ($S_A$) to characterize state spreading and distinguish between thermal and scar states in time evolution.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by the one-dimensional anyon-Hubbard model, characterized by a Hamiltonian involving hopping terms and an on-site interaction $U$, with statistical phase $	heta$ governing particle statistics (bosonic, fermionic, or fractional).
key_observables: Krylov Complexity ($C_K(t)$), Entanglement Entropy ($S_A$), Fidelity ($F(t)$), and the saturation plateau value of complexity.
important_parameters: Statistical phase ($	heta$), on-site interaction strength ($U$), hopping amplitude ($J$), and system size ($L$).
main_assumptions: The analysis involves constructing exact many-body scar eigenstates and analyzing dynamics in different regimes (strong vs. weak interaction).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the scaling of entanglement entropy for thermal versus scar states, and show time evolution plots of $C_K(t)$ confirming perfect revivals or saturation depending on quench parameters.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the anyon-Hubbard model and its Hamiltonian. It then develops diagnostics like Krylov complexity and scar state construction. Key results are presented by analyzing dynamics under different conditions, such as no quench vs. quench, and varying interaction strengths.
why_interesting: This work provides a sophisticated tool (Krylov complexity) to probe non-equilibrium dynamics in systems with exotic statistics, linking topological properties (anyons) directly to quantum information measures of complexity.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic illustration of the anyon-Hubbard model. The hopping amplitude depends on the particle occupation number of the left site.

FIG. 2. Distribution and finite-size scaling of the entangle- ment entropy SA. (a) SA as a function of the eigenenergy E for L = 10. The blue open circles represent highly entangled states in the N = L subspace, while the red stars denote the exact scar states in the M = 0, 1, · · · , L subspace, with the circle-star symbol indicating the scar state that lies in the N = L subspace. (b) Scaling of SA of the scar states (circle- star symbols in (a)) at filling N/L = 1 as a function of the system size L. SA does not grow linearly with increasing L, but instead follows a logarithmic scaling relation. The red line shows the asymptotic analytical curve 1

FIG. 3. Time evolution of scar states in Krylov space for dif- ferent lattice sizes L = 10, 12, 14. Panels (a) and (b) show the fidelity F(t) and Krylov complexity CK(t), respectively, while panels (c) and (d) display the Lanczos coefficients an and bn. Open circles denote the numerical results obtained from exact diagonalization, while solid lines represent the an- alytical predictions. The hopping amplitude and interaction strength are set to J = 1 and U = 1, respectively.

FIG. 4. Quench dynamics of the Krylov complexity CK(t). The four panels correspond to different initial-state statisti- cal phases: (a) θi = 0; (b) θi = π/2; (c) θi = 2π/3; and (d) θi = π. In each panel, the statistical phase is quenched to θf = sπ/12 (s = 0, 1, 6, 7, 8, 11, 12). In the absence of a quench, i.e., when θf = θi throughout the time evolution, CK(t) remains very small over long times and exhibits os- cillations, characteristic of perfect scar dynamics. When θf is close to θi, CK(t) increases with time while retaining pro- nounced oscillations, signaling approximate scar dynamics. The system size is L = 8, with J = 0.1 and U = 1.

FIG. 5. Time evolution of the Krylov complexity CK(t) in the regime J = 10 and U = 1. Panels (a)-(d) cor- respond to the initial-state statistical phases θi = 0, π/2, 2π/3, and π, respectively. In each panel, the statistical phase of the post-quench Hamiltonian is set to θf = sπ/12 (s = 0, 1, 6, 7, 8, 11, 12). CK(t) increases over a short time scale and saturates to a high plateau for all quenches, except for the exact scar case without a quench, θf = θi. The system size is L = 8.
